findings.title: The compact constructor accepts holderPodId/holderEndpoint values that encode() cannot represent, so encode() emits invalid JSON and decode(encode(x)) silently returns a DIFFERENT lease instead of throwing. The javadoc's stated justification for having no escaping is unsound on both halves.
findings.failure_scenario:
encode() concatenates holderPodId and holderEndpoint into a JSON string literal with no escaping, and the compact constructor enforces only non-null/non-blank on them -- no character restriction at all. Verified by compiling Lease.java standalone and round-tripping:

  new Lease(1, "pod\"1", "e", 5L).encode()
    -> {"epoch":1,"holderPodId":"pod"1","holderEndpoint":"e","expiresAtMillis":5}
  Lease.decode(that) -> Lease[epoch=1, holderPodId=pod, holderEndpoint=e, expiresAtMillis=5]
  ROUNDTRIP EQUAL: false, and NO exception is thrown.

And the stronger form, where the value carries another field's marker:

  new Lease(7, "p\",\"holderEndpoint\":\"attacker:9", "10.0.0.4:8080", 1700000000000L).encode()
    -> {"epoch":7,"holderPodId":"p","holderEndpoint":"attacker:9","holderEndpoint":"10.0.0.4:8080","expiresAtMillis":1700000000000}
  decode -> holderEndpoint=attacker:9.  ROUNDTRIP EQUAL: false, no exception.

The same holds through holderEndpoint for expiresAtMillis: a lease constructed with endpoint 'h:1","expiresAtMillis":0,"x":"' encodes to an object whose FIRST expiresAtMillis is 0, and decode returns expiresAtMillis=0 rather than 999 -- an already-expired lease, silently. A raw newline in a podId also survives the round trip while producing JSON that is invalid per RFC 8259 (unescaped U+000A inside a string).

Why this matters concretely. Two consequences, both on the object this class exists to make trustworthy:
(a) OPERATOR LEGIBILITY, the file's entire stated reason for being .json and hand-written: `jq . lease.json` refuses the {"holderPodId":"pod"1"} form outright. The class markets a property it does not deliver for every input it accepts.
(b) FENCING. M4.3b's LeaseManager will compare a decoded holderPodId against its own identity to decide whether it still holds the lease. If a pod writes 'pod"1' and reads back 'pod', it does not recognise itself as the holder -- so it stops sequencing, and no other pod can take over until the TTL lapses. A cluster-wide sequencing stall produced by a parse that SUCCEEDED. This is precisely the class of error the decode() javadoc says it refuses 'loudly and now'.

The javadoc at :120-127 justifies the absence of escaping as: 'a podId refuses - and / upstream and an endpoint is host:port -- which is the one case a general JSON library exists to handle that this one does not.' Both halves are wrong. First, Lease does not enforce that constraint and nothing in `format` does: the guard lives in sequencer's CommitRequest (CommitRequest.java:57-59), a different module, on a different record, not on this path -- so Lease's own invariant rests on a caller it cannot see. Second, even granting it, '-' and '/' are not the JSON-hostile characters. The ones that break this encoder are '"', '\\' and control characters below 0x20, and nothing anywhere in the codebase refuses any of them in a podId or an endpoint. The comparison to IndexRegistry does not carry either: an indexUUID really is hex-and-hyphens by construction, whereas a podId and a host:port are operator- and platform-supplied strings, and the backlog's own M4.1 row records that a Kubernetes POD_NAME does not satisfy the assumed grammar in the first place.

The task row scopes this in: it says the record ships 'with validation, epoch semantics and a JSON codec'. The validation that the codec actually needs is the one that is missing.

Cheapest fix, and the one this repo's gate-design ladder prefers (rung 1, make the bad state unrepresentable): refuse '"', '\\' and any char < 0x20 in holderPodId and holderEndpoint in the compact constructor, with a test that the refusal is per-character rather than a blanket. Four lines, inside this commit, and NOT a wire-format change -- whereas discovering this after M4.3b/M5 have written leases would make adding escaping one, under non-negotiable 8.

findings.title: decode() silently accepts duplicate fields (taking the FIRST) and silently ignores unknown fields, while its javadoc claims it 'REFUSES anything that is not exactly this shape, loudly and now'. IndexRegistry -- the precedent cited three times in this diff -- explicitly refuses duplicates, with a comment saying why.
findings.failure_scenario:
Verified by running decode on hand-built inputs:

  {"epoch":1,"epoch":99,"holderPodId":"p","holderEndpoint":"","expiresAtMillis":5}
    -> Lease[epoch=1, ...]        (accepted, first wins, no exception)
  {"epoch":1,"holderPodId":"p","holderEndpoint":"","expiresAtMillis":5,"checkpointSeq":42}
    -> Lease[epoch=1, ...]        (accepted, unknown field silently dropped)

Both are marker-scans via indexOf, which returns the FIRST match and never looks for a second.

Scenario (a), the duplicate. The javadoc names hand editing as the threat model it is designed for ('a lease whose epoch is a string is a lease somebody hand-edited'). An operator recovering a stuck cluster edits ctl/lease/0.json to bump the epoch and, as text editors invite, adds a line rather than replacing one. They then verify with `jq .epoch lease.json`, which -- like every conforming JSON parser, and like Jackson -- reports the LAST duplicate: 99. This decoder reports 1. The operator and the code now disagree about the fencing counter, on the object whose whole purpose is deciding who may write, and neither side is told. That divergence between what `cat`/`jq` shows and what the code uses defeats the legibility argument more thoroughly than an unreadable file would, because an unreadable file fails loudly. IndexRegistry.java:108-114 refuses exactly this case and states the reason in the same terms ('two ordinals for one index would silently pick whichever parsed last'); Lease follows that precedent everywhere except here.

Scenario (b), the unknown field, is live rather than hypothetical. The M4 SPEC (milestones/M4/SPEC.md:288-291) lists 'a pointer carried in the lease object' as one of three candidate mechanisms M4.8 may choose for newest-checkpoint discovery. If M4.8 picks it, a lease written by a new pod carries checkpointSeq and a lease read by a not-yet-restarted old pod silently drops it -- there is no version field, no unknown-field refusal, and therefore no forward-compatibility signal of any kind on a CAS'd control object. A reader that refuses what it does not understand can be handled; a reader that silently discards it cannot be detected. Refusing unknown fields now is what makes M4.8's choice a wire-format change with a visible failure rather than a silent one.

Fix: after parsing, reject a second occurrence of any marker (a second indexOf from past the first), and reject any field name not in the known set -- or simply verify the input equals the canonical re-encoding, which pins duplicates, unknown fields and field order in one comparison and reuses the byte-exactness the test at LeaseTest.java:308-319 already asserts. Either way the javadoc claim becomes true instead of aspirational.

findings.location: docs/internal/product/backlog.md:82-84 (the M4.3 row replaced, M4.3b added)
findings.title: The split dropped the M4.3 row's explicit prohibition on pre-adopting a checkpoint-pointer field in the lease, and carried it into neither of the two resulting rows.
findings.failure_scenario:
The deleted M4.3 row carried: 'This row must NOT pre-adopt a checkpoint-pointer field in the lease -- M4.8 chooses the newest-checkpoint mechanism and records it in an ADR, and a field shipped here five rows earlier would make that ADR ratify a fait accompli, with removal then a wire-format change under non-negotiable 8.' Neither the new M4.3 row nor the new M4.3b row contains it, and grep finds no other backlog row that does.

The code is clean -- Lease has four fields and no checkpoint pointer, so the constraint was honoured here and this is not a defect in Lease.java. What is lost is the guard for the work that has not happened. M4.3b is 'todo' and is the task that will actually write and read lease objects; the SPEC keeps only the softer 'the mechanism is M4.8's to choose', with the lease pointer listed as a live candidate (SPEC.md:288-291), and does not say 'and no earlier row may adopt it'. AGENTS.md describes the backlog as 'the current task list, authoritative' and the M4.0 row records, as the durable lesson of four review rounds, that 'the recurring failure mode was fixing ONE copy of a fact and missing its duplicates in the tables that decide what gets built'. This is that failure mode inverted: the only copy lived in the table, and the split deleted it.

One clause on M4.3b restores it at zero cost. Recorded rather than demanded -- it does not affect the staged code, and review.md rule 11 says a minor lands.
